h1: Choosing which states to sell in after your home state
title: Choosing Your Next State to Sell Beer In | Craft Beer School
desc: How a craft brewery should rank Indian states for its first expansion: registration effort, price, route to market and cold chain.
teaser: Your second state will cost more time and cash than your first. Choose it with a spreadsheet, not a map.
standfirst: Selling beer outside your home state means a new set of registrations, a new tax structure and often a new route to market. Some states pay back quickly. Others tie up cash for a year. Here is how we would rank them.
sections: Every new state is a new market with its own rules

Inside your home state you know the excise officer, the distributors and the price list. Cross a border and almost all of that resets. Beer moving between Indian states typically needs an export permit from the home state and an import permit in the destination. Your label and brand often need registering again. Duty is set by the destination state. Some states sell through a state-run corporation, Karnataka's KSBCL and Tamil Nadu's TASMAC being the familiar examples, while others use private distributors and retailers.

Rules and fees vary by state and change, so check the current notifications or work with a licensing consultant before committing a single keg. Our overview of craft beer rules by state sets out the questions to ask.
Score states on five things, not one

Founders tend to pick the state with the biggest city or the loudest craft scene. That is one factor out of five. We rank candidates on a simple sheet:

  1. Drinker base. Is there a population already paying for craft or premium beer in on-trade and retail?
  2. Shelf price after duty. Work out your beer's likely retail price in that state. If it lands far above the imported premium lagers there, volume will be thin.
  3. Entry cost and time. Registration fees, label approvals and the months before first sale.
  4. Payment cycle. How long between dispatch and cash? A state corporation or a distributor paying in 60 to 90 days ties up working capital.
  5. Distance and cold chain. How many hours by truck and can the beer stay cold?

Give each a score of one to five, weight them for your business and add them up. The sheet is less about precision than about forcing the argument into the open.
Run the price backwards from the shelf

The single most useful calculation is a reverse price build. Start with the price a drinker would pay for a 650 ml bottle or a 500 ml can in that state. Subtract retailer margin, distributor margin and state duty as published. What is left is your ex-brewery price.

If that figure is below your cost per litre plus freight, the state does not work at that shelf price. You either accept a higher shelf price and lower volume or you wait. We see founders skip this step, ship a full truck and then find their beer sitting 30% above every competitor on the shelf. The working takes an afternoon. A failed launch takes a year to recover from.
Freight and heat decide what you can send

Unpasteurised craft beer does not like a 1,500 km journey in a non-refrigerated truck in May. Ambient trailers in central India can run above 40 °C. Hop aroma fades fast at that temperature and oxidation shows up within weeks.

Practical choices follow from this. Neighbouring states with short transit times usually make better first moves than distant ones. Packaged beer travels better than kegs because the logistics of returning empty kegs over long distances are painful. A keg that costs ₹8,000 to replace and comes back once a quarter instead of once a month quietly doubles the capital you have tied up in steel. If you must ship far, budget for refrigerated freight from day one and price it into the shelf calculation above.
Start with one city and one partner

Treat a new state as a pilot. Pick one city, one distributor or one key account group and a small range, two or three beers at most. Agree what success means in units per month after six months. A clear exit line helps too: if you are not at half the target by month six, you stop shipping new stock.

Founders who launch in three states at once spread their sales time and working capital too thin to learn anything. One state done well teaches you the process. The second is faster.

Choose the partner as carefully as the state. Ask a prospective distributor which craft or premium brands they already carry, how many cold rooms they run and how often their reps visit each outlet. Ask two of their existing suppliers how quickly they get paid. A distributor with a warm warehouse and slow payment will undo a good state choice within one season.
Put the numbers in your model before you visit

Before you travel, add each candidate state as its own column in your financial model: entry costs, months to first sale, ex-brewery price, freight per litre, payment days and expected volume. Look at peak cash need, not only margin.

This is the part a guide can only outline. Building the model, testing it against real duty schedules and deciding what the brewery can afford to lock up is what we work through properly in the course.

Your first step: pick your two most likely states and do the reverse price build for one beer in each. If the ex-brewery price does not cover your cost plus freight, you have saved yourself a trip.
faqs: What permits does beer need to move between Indian states?

Usually an export permit from the home state and an import permit in the destination state, plus brand or label registration there. Requirements vary by state and change, so check current notifications.
Should a craft brewery expand to a neighbouring state first?
Often yes. Shorter transit keeps beer fresher, freight cheaper and visits easier, though the shelf price and payment cycle in that state still need to work.
How long does it take to start selling in a new state?
It varies widely with the state's registration process. Plan for several months between applying and first sale. Model the cash that ties up.
